passage.text:
School libraries notice
The school libraries team needs helpers on Saturday. Bring gloves and arrive before nine.

Message from a friend
I have booked the reading corners session for Tuesday, but I may arrive late. Please start without me and save a place.

Information sign
Visitors to the school libraries may use the tools, but they must return them before leaving.

Short announcement
The students meeting has moved from Room 2 to Room 4 because the first room is being painted.

Notice for members
Members can borrow one reading corners guide for a week. Ask at the desk if you need another copy.

passage.text: The people below want to choose from school library activities. Decide which option is most suitable.

passage.label: A
passage.text: After school reading buddy — A weekday afternoon programme where adult volunteers read aloud with pupils in the second year, one child at a time. Training lasts one hour, no computer skills are needed, and sessions run between three and five. Volunteers meet the same child each week, which builds confidence quickly.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Puppet story time for toddlers — A free Friday morning session for children under five, with puppets, songs and picture books. No booking is needed, parents stay with their child, and the room grows noisy as children join in the stories. It ends with a sticker for every child, and older siblings are welcome too.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Book mending workshop — A weekend half-day class where you learn to repair torn books with new spines and clean pages. Groups stay small, every tool is supplied, and beginners finish with three techniques they can use at home. The teacher demonstrates each step, and you keep the books you practise on.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Library app coaching — A free drop-in session where staff help you use the school library app to borrow ebooks and renew loans. Bring your own device, join on weekday lunchtimes, and follow the steps at your own speed with a helper beside you. No appointment is needed, and the service is open to all ages.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Multilingual book circle — An evening club where members read a story in six different languages and take turns choosing the next book. Tea and biscuits are served, conversation is lively, and each member is expected to finish one novel a month. Newcomers are welcome, but regular attendance matters to the group.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Silent study room with exam desk — A silent study room open until ten at night, with desks that students reserve in advance and revision guides kept on shelves inside. Only enrolled students may enter, and phones must stay switched off while inside. Late-evening demand is high, so desks often book out several days ahead.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Holiday reading quest — A six-week summer challenge for readers aged twelve to sixteen, where points are collected through an app and prizes go to the ten highest scorers. Each week offers a fresh reading list, and finishing any book earns double points. A celebration event at the end marks every reader who completes the quest.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Early book sorting shift — An early shift that shelves donated books before the school opens, with heavy boxes arriving on some mornings. No experience is needed, shifts run on weekdays from seven to nine, and volunteers work on their own or in pairs. A member of staff stays nearby to answer questions during the shift.

questions.prompt: Grace has just retired and wants to help young pupils with their reading on weekday afternoons. She prefers quiet one-to-one work, has no computer skills, and would like a little training first.
Hugo has a three-year-old daughter and wants a free morning activity they can attend without booking. She loves puppets and songs, and he does not mind a noisy, lively room.
Elena is studying for her final exams and needs a quiet place to work late in the evening. She wants to reserve a desk, keep her phone off, and have revision guides close by.
Marco is fourteen and wants a challenge for the school holidays that earns prizes. He enjoys using apps, reads quickly, and would like clear weekly goals with something to celebrate at the end.
Ivy wants to learn how to repair damaged library books as a weekend hobby. She is a complete beginner, would like small class sizes, and wants to use tools supplied by the library.

passage.text: When the students in our town started a school libraries project, few residents expected it to grow so quickly. At first, the organisers met in a small room and planned one simple activity involving reading corners. They soon discovered that people were more willing to join when they could see a clear benefit for the neighbourhood. The organisers therefore published a short timetable and invited local businesses to offer practical help.

The project was not completely easy. Some volunteers were worried that the work would take too much time, while others wanted to change the plan every week. The team solved this by giving each person one small responsibility and reviewing the results together. This made the project feel manageable, and it also meant that new volunteers could contribute without special experience.

Looking back, the organiser says the most important lesson was not the final result but the way people learned to cooperate. The group still has problems, especially when the weather affects outdoor work, yet members now discuss solutions rather than blaming one another. For this reason, the project has become a useful example of how a modest local idea can create lasting connections.

parts.passageTitle: Part 4 – The Students' Library Plan Grows

passage.text: Sixth-form students noticed the school library was almost empty after lessons, although many pupils stayed late for clubs. They surveyed two hundred students and found most would use it if it stayed open. The head teacher agreed to a one-month trial if they organised the timetable. (16) ..... They posted the plan on the library noticeboard and asked users to comment after the first week.

The trial began in January, with the library open until six on three evenings. Two students volunteered each evening to unlock the door and switch on the lights. A furniture shop donated four beanbag chairs and a small shelf for graphic novels. (17) ..... A parent then donated a second-hand lamp, making the new reading corner feel warmer.

Within a fortnight, attendance grew from eight students to thirty-five, and the beanbags were always taken first. The team introduced a quiet zone near the windows and a discussion area by the door. The chess club could finally stop working on the floor. (18) ..... The club moved into the discussion area, while readers beside the windows could continue without interruption.

The main difficulty came when two students argued over a laptop borrowed from the IT department. The team realised they needed rules for shared equipment, so they wrote an agreement and asked every user to sign it. The IT teacher offered two more laptops if everyone followed it. (19) ..... No further disagreements about equipment were reported during the remainder of the trial.

After the trial, the head teacher made the evening opening permanent because attendance exceeded expectations. The team planned the next term and invited younger pupils to suggest books. Parents said their children now chose the library over the corridor. (20) ..... The library assistant said she had not seen the room so full in twelve years. Younger students soon joined the evening teams, proving that the project could continue after its original organisers had left school.

passage.label: G

passage.label: H

parts.passageTitle: Part 5 – Reading Corner Sessions on Saturdays

passage.text: The students usually meet (21) ........ Saturday. New members are shown how to (22) ........ the equipment. They can ask for advice if they are (23) ........ about a task. The group works together (24) ........ everyone can learn. Members often share ideas (25) ........ the session. The project has become a popular way to meet (26) ........ people. The new reading sessions are open to students who want to discover different kinds of books. Each week, a volunteer introduces a short activity and gives readers time to share their opinions. Some students prefer stories, while others enjoy information books, but everyone is encouraged to recommend something for the next session. Teachers noticed that students who rarely borrowed books began joining the sessions. The activities are short enough to fit into a normal school week, but they give everyone time to talk about characters, facts and new words. Suggestions from students are added to a list for future meetings.

parts.passageTitle: Part 6 – Reading Corners Kept in Order

passage.text: The students meet (27) ........ week to plan activities. New members learn (28) ........ to use the reading corners safely. They can join the work, (29) ........ they should follow the group’s instructions. The project has kept useful materials (30) ........ being thrown away. It is a place (31) ........ people can exchange ideas. Remember (32) ........ ask for help when you need it. Keeping the reading corner tidy is now a shared responsibility. Students return books to labelled shelves, report damaged copies and leave the tables ready for the following group. The library team checks the area regularly and changes the display when a new topic becomes popular. The team also keeps a record of popular titles and replaces damaged books when money is available. This careful routine means that the corner remains useful for new classes as well as the students who helped create it.
